source.title: Scaling Laws for Online Advertisement Retrieval
source.authors: Yunli Wang; Zhen Zhang; Zi-Xuan Yang; Tian-Yu Xu; Zhiqiang Wang; Yu Li; Ru-Fan Zhou; Zhi-Qiang Liu; Yan-Jie Zhu; Jian Yang; Shiyang Wen; Peng Jiang

page_placements.theme: Scaling-related quality gains can extend to productivity and revenue

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling relationships in online advertisement retrieval, a different task and training setting from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures FLOPs against the retrieval metric R/R* and, in two deployments, checks estimated against actual online revenue gains. It does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy, language-model tokens, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. The plotted scaling-curve data points are figure-only; numeric fit R2 values are stated in text or captions. A/B results about R/R* as a revenue surrogate and model-design applications are not language-model loss results.
record.test_reason: The study tests scaling in advertising retrieval, bearing on V5. It fits a flexible broken power-law relationship between FLOPs and retrieval performance across three architecture families and two scenes. It does not establish the same single power-law form as language-model loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors report broken scaling relationships between FLOPs and R/R* within each tested architecture and scene, and use them with revenue calibration and machine-cost simulation for system optimisation. Their applications achieve a reported combined 5.1% online revenue gain. They acknowledge a narrower compute range than NLP studies and architecture-specific parameters. Their conclusions do not establish a universal unbroken power law.
record.recipe_differences: Uses industrial advertising retrieval models and the R/R* metric against FLOPs, fitting a broken neural scaling law. It does not use language-model held-out cross-entropy or sweep parameter count, token count, and compute jointly.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling parameters differ by architecture; experiments use different scenes and retrieval stages. The MLP Scene1 plotted curve is a representative main-text example, with additional fits in the appendix.

fits_no_version.finding: Two feature-expanded MLPs yield revenue gains of 0.38% and 0.69%, versus predictions of 0.33% and 0.62%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A composite scaling-law and revenue-surrogate estimator can predict modest deployment revenue gains when input features expand.

fits_no_version.finding: R/R* correlates with online revenue, with R² = 0.902 in pre-ranking and 0.725 in matching; correlation varies with the metric's top-m setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Revenue-weighted offline retrieval metrics can predict online advertising revenue, with accuracy depending on stage and metric settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix E.1 reports substantial degradation for an unreasonable layer allocation, illustrated by [3328, 1024, 32, 32, 32, 1], without a numerical controlled comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer allocation can affect advertising retrieval performance at a given FLOPs budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Four scaling-guided system optimisations produce reported revenue gains of 0.85%, 1.0%, 2.8%, and 0.45%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-guided model selection and resource allocation can improve production advertising revenue.

record.problems: The scaling outcomes use R/R*, not held-out loss; the work covers a narrower compute range than large NLP scaling studies. Individual plotted data values are not stated, and the reported fit statistics do not provide uncertainty intervals. The paper's online revenue validation is limited to two MLP models.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss and its dependence on parameters, tokens, and compute.
Small-run loss fits predicting runs orders of magnitude larger; the revenue checks do not test this.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocations as powers of a fixed training-compute budget.
Controlled architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count. Appendix E.1 discusses allocation at given FLOPs instead.
Other modalities and regimes beyond the tested advertising models; whether a single power law suffices; generalisation outside the observed compute range.
Downstream task performance predicted from a separate pretraining scale or pretraining loss; these are direct retrieval-performance fits and revenue-surrogate checks.

Sensitivity of estimated exponents or compute-optimal splits to fitting choices and training setup. No fitted exponents, controlled sensitivity comparisons, or single-versus-broken-law comparison are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The single-model rows are constituent observations, not independent demonstrations of a scaling law. Their unreadable coordinates do not negate the explicitly reported family-level fits. High in-sample R² for a flexible BNSL neither demonstrates upward extrapolation nor proves that a single power law fails. The narrow tested range and small revenue-prediction errors alone do not warrant the record's additional limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, and compute is not measured.
The study does not test predictions from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute optimum over parameter and token counts is studied.
It does not compare depth, width, and architecture at a fixed parameter count. Appendix E.1 discusses unit allocation at given FLOPs but does not provide a controlled fixed-parameter comparison.
Tests advertising retrieval models and R/R* versus FLOPs, not image/video modalities, repeated data, or transfer. It does not test whether language-model cross-entropy has the same form.
Online advertising revenue is not downstream language-model task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.

The study uses broken neural scaling-law fits and notes architecture-specific parameters, but does not vary fitting choices or quantify exponent dependence, nor test a compute-optimal parameter/token split.
